title: The End of “As-Is”: Could AI Undermine Software’s U.S. Legal Shield?
gist: CSIS argues that cheap AI vulnerability discovery — $8.80 per automated exploit run, 21 unknown FFmpeg bugs for roughly $1,000 in compute — collapses the economic assumption behind software's "as-is" liability shield under the Learned Hand negligence formula, and calls for congressional action creating safe harbors for firms following NIST's SSDF while targeting liability at willful inaction.

insights.claim: The software industry cannot simultaneously market AI as reliably identifying major vulnerability classes before shipment and claim that software defects are inherently unforeseeable, which is the premise of its broad legal immunity.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Vendors' own AI security marketing is building the evidentiary record for future liability claims against them.
insights.quote: Either AI can reliably identify major classes of vulnerabilities before products ship, or software defects remain an inherently unforeseeable reality that justifies broad legal immunity.
insights.locator: The software industry cannot have it both ways

insights.claim: Vendors lead with AI security capability in earnings calls and product announcements and pitch it to shareholders as a competitive advantage, which is precisely what undermines their liability defense.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Public AI-security claims made to investors create legal exposure; expect disclosure language around AI security capability to become more hedged.
insights.quote: Vendors are not hiding this new capability. They lead with it in earnings calls and product announcements, and they pitch it to customers and shareholders as a competitive advantage.
insights.locator: Vendors are not hiding this new capability

insights.claim: The March 2026 Cyber Strategy dropped the 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy's software liability-shifting proposal in favor of deregulation and voluntary private sector action, just as AI was strengthening the case for liability.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: U.S. federal policy is currently moving away from software liability, so near-term regulatory risk to vendors is low even as the intellectual case strengthens.
insights.quote: In March 2026, the new Cyber Strategy dropped that proposal entirely in favor of deregulation and voluntary private sector action instead.
insights.locator: The 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy proposed shifting liability

insights.claim: Software escapes strict product liability because courts and legislators treat it as a licensed service rather than a product, letting it operate under contract law while lamps, cars, and harnesses fall under tort.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The service-versus-product classification is the single legal hinge; any reclassification would transfer enormous risk onto software vendors' balance sheets.
insights.quote: Courts and legislators treat software as a licensed service rather than a product, letting it hide behind contract law instead.

insights.claim: The information technology sector commands more than 36 percent of the S&P 500's total market weight, invalidating the 1990s premise that a fragile nascent tech industry needed a legal shield to survive litigation costs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Index concentration is now itself a political argument for regulating software, and a 36 percent index weight means any liability regime change is a market-level event.
insights.quote: An information technology sector that commands more than 36 percent of the S&P 500’s total market weight is no longer a fragile infant in need of a legal shield.

insights.claim: Courts accepted lower standards for software because exhaustive testing of tens of millions of lines of code with trillions of execution paths was mathematically impossible for human teams, while a car has roughly 30,000 physical parts.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The complexity defense is the load-bearing legal argument; AI tooling that can stress test millions of paths simultaneously is what removes it.
insights.quote: While a car has roughly 30,000 physical parts, software contains tens of millions of lines of code with trillions of execution paths.

insights.claim: All three justifications for software's legal exceptionalism rest on a single assumption, that finding defects before shipment costs too much to demand, and frontier AI breaks that assumption.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Identifies the single point of failure in software's liability architecture, which is why a cost collapse in vulnerability discovery is a legal event, not just a technical one.
insights.quote: All three justifications rest on one assumption: that finding defects before shipment costs too much to demand it.
insights.locator: All three justifications rest on one assumption

themes.theme: The economics of AI bug hunting

insights.claim: Google's Project Zero and DeepMind unveiled Big Sleep in late 2024, an AI agent that found a zero-day in SQLite, one of the most obsessively audited codebases and embedded in billions of devices.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Proof that AI agents find defects human auditors missed in the most-scrutinized code, the empirical basis for the whole liability argument.
insights.quote: Google’s Project Zero and DeepMind unveiled “Big Sleep,” an AI agent that uncovered a zero-day flaw in SQLite, a database engine embedded in billions of devices and renowned for being one of the most obsessively audited codebases.
insights.locator: In late 2024, Google's Project Zero and DeepMind

insights.claim: By mid-2025 Big Sleep escalated from catching unreleased bugs to thwarting an active zero-day exploit in the wild moments before threat actors could weaponize it.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Marks the transition of AI security agents from research demo to operational defense, which is when the reasonableness standard shifts.
insights.quote: By mid-2025, Big Sleep escalated from catching unreleased bugs to thwarting an active zero-day exploit in the wild moments before threat actors could weaponize it.

insights.claim: University of Illinois researchers showed automated exploit attempts against real-world vulnerabilities cost as little as $8.80 per run using off-the-shelf models such as GPT-4, a fraction of human security researcher cost.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The precise per-run cost is what flips the Learned Hand burden term toward negligence; it also implies attacker economics are equally cheap.
insights.quote: running automated exploit attempts against real-world vulnerabilities costs as little as $8.80 per run using off-the-shelf models such as GPT-4
insights.locator: University of Illinois researchers evaluating AI security agents

insights.claim: A security startup called Depthfirst used a commercially available model to surface 21 previously unknown vulnerabilities in FFmpeg for roughly $1,000 in total compute, without any multi-billion-dollar custom research lab.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Shows frontier vulnerability discovery is available to any small firm off commercial models, meaning the capability is commoditized not proprietary.
insights.quote: A security startup called Depthfirst used a commercially available model to surface 21 previously unknown vulnerabilities in FFmpeg, a piece of software embedded in an enormous share of the internet’s video infrastructure, for roughly $1,000 in total compute.

insights.claim: AI cuts the overall cost of routine software engineering by 30 to 50 percent, which frees capital that easily covers continuous AI verification while still expanding profit margins.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A 30 to 50 percent engineering cost reduction is the margin-expansion number underlying software AI theses, and it removes the security-versus-margin trade-off excuse.
insights.quote: it slashes the overall cost of routine software engineering by 30–50 percent

insights.claim: Security budgets typically represent under 11 percent of enterprise cyber spending because vendors historically starved them to protect core engineering margins.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A baseline spend figure; any liability regime shift would drive this share upward, a demand tailwind for security tooling vendors.
insights.quote: Historically, vendors starved security budgets, which typically represent under 11 percent of enterprise cyber spending, to protect core engineering margins.
insights.locator: The total economics of building software

themes.theme: Learned Hand and the closing window

insights.claim: Under the Learned Hand formula from United States v. Carroll Towing, negligence occurs when the burden of precautions is less than the probability of harm times its gravity, and software vendors won that equation by default for 70 years because manual code auditing cost far more than any individual bug's expected harm.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A concrete legal test that can be recomputed with new cost data, which is why AI cost collapse translates directly into legal exposure.
insights.quote: A party is negligent when the burden of precautions (B) is less than the probability of harm (P) multiplied by the gravity of that harm (L). In other words, negligence occurs when B < P x L.

insights.claim: Applying an as-is disclaimer after running, or declining to run, a low-cost precautionary scan that the company itself markets as effective is negligence in substance even if not yet in doctrine.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Flags a live litigation theory that plaintiffs could deploy before any statute changes, particularly against vendors selling into critical infrastructure.
insights.quote: Under the formula’s own terms, that is negligence in substance, even if not yet in doctrine.

insights.claim: The same automation making bug hunting cheap for defenders will make exploit development cheap for attackers, so whoever automates first keeps the advantage and left alone the market pushes that race toward the attacker.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A time-limited window argument: the defensive cost advantage is temporary, which raises urgency for security spend and for policy action.
insights.quote: Whoever automates first keeps the advantage. Left alone, the market pushes that race toward the attacker.

insights.claim: Competitive dynamics ensure freed-up AI savings will not be spent on security voluntarily, because in a competitive market the vendor that pockets the savings wins and the vendor that spends them on unrequired security does not.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Explains why voluntary private-sector action, the stated policy of the March 2026 Cyber Strategy, will not produce the security outcome it assumes.
insights.quote: In a competitive market, the vendor that pockets the savings wins; the vendor that spends the savings on security nobody requires does not.
insights.locator: But freed-up capital does not spend itself on defense

insights.claim: Courts have little appetite to unwind decades of enforced boilerplate case by case and jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction change would produce years of unpredictable litigation, which is the argument for legislative rather than judicial action.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The realistic transmission channel is Congress, not the courts, so watch legislative signals rather than case law for timing.
insights.quote: That is the argument for legislative action: Congress can update the assumption on purpose, and on a deliberate timeline, instead of leaving it to a slow accumulation of individual lawsuits to do it by accident.
insights.locator: None of this happens on its own

insights.claim: The European Union's revised Product Liability Directive, adopted in 2024, formally classifies software as a product, with enforcement beginning once member states transpose it by the end of 2026.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A hard end-2026 date for EU software product liability exposure that will hit U.S. vendors selling into Europe regardless of U.S. policy direction.
insights.quote: Its revised Product Liability Directive, adopted in 2024, formally classifies software as a product, though enforcement will not begin until member states transpose it by the end of 2026.
insights.locator: Internationally, the European Union has made the same conceptual leap

insights.claim: Congress should codify safe harbors granting protection from punitive damages to producers that follow NIST's Secure Software Development Framework, document AI-assisted security testing, and maintain risk-based remediation.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: SSDF compliance would become the effective legal standard, driving demand for documented AI security testing and attestation tooling.
insights.quote: The goal should be to reward diligence, not punish every residual bug.

insights.claim: Liability exposure should target willful blindness rather than ordinary imperfection, focusing on firms that decline standard automated scanning, ignore high-confidence findings, or repeatedly ship known failure modes into critical infrastructure.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defines the narrow exposure band, which limits the systemic cost of reform and makes passage more plausible than broad strict liability.
insights.quote: Legal exposure should focus on willful blindness, not ordinary imperfection.

insights.claim: Any liability framework should shield volunteer open-source maintainers while placing responsibility on the commercial vendors that package, deploy, and profit from software without basic automated due diligence.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Commercial integrators absorb the liability, which raises compliance costs for enterprise software packagers relative to upstream open-source projects.
insights.quote: Liability should rest primarily with the firms that package, deploy, and profit from software without conducting basic automated due diligence.
insights.locator: Protect open-source maintainers while holding commercial integrators responsible

insights.claim: Policymakers need not invent a new theory of software liability because the Office of the National Cyber Director's 2024 symposia mapped the policy architecture and NIST's SSDF already provides a practical baseline.
insights.speaker: CSIS
entities: Office of the National Cyber Director
insights.so_what: Low implementation friction means a policy reversal could move fast if the political mood shifts after a major incident.
insights.quote: Policymakers do not need to invent a new theory of software liability, nor should they demand flawless code.
